tier_reason: The README only asserts that Harper lints 'in milliseconds' where LanguageTool 'would take several seconds' and uses 'less than 1/50th' of its memory; no measured latency, document size, hardware or harness is given anywhere. The repo's own Criterion benches (harper-core/benches/parse_essay.rs, spellcheck.rs) time Harper alone and never run LanguageTool, so the speed claim is directional only.

corrections.caveats: Author assertion only: no benchmark against LanguageTool exists in the repo or (per a WebSearch, snippet only) anywhere public; 'milliseconds' and 'several seconds' are not measurements, and the 1/50th figure is memory, not latency. harper-core/benches (parse_essay.rs, lint_essay, spellcheck.rs) and harper-wasm/benches/wasm_bench.js time Harper alone (the wasm harness reuses the native word lists so wasm and native could be compared, but no numbers are published). The claim is not wasm-versus-native: the baseline is a native Java tool and the claim is about the native Rust engine, so it fits this category poorly. Harper covers far fewer rules than LanguageTool (a forum commenter, snippet only) and supports English only, so the work done per document is not equal.

notes: Real, notable project (16.3k stars, Apache-2.0, last commit 2026-10-11) but the speed claim has no numbers, so it drops from C to D; keep and document per the keep-and-document rule. Shortcomings: no LanguageTool benchmark, unequal rule coverage, claim is native-versus-Java rather than wasm-versus-native or wasm-versus-JS (off-category baseline).

tier_reason: First-party Google tables in tfjs-backend-wasm/README.md (Chrome 79, averaged over 200 runs) compare the WASM backend against the in-browser plain JS backend; the harness is public (e2e/benchmarks/local-benchmark) but the devices are named without CPU models and no compiler or flags are given, so it falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README text: for MobileNet V2 the WASM backend is 'between ~3X-11.5X faster than the plain JS backend' and '~5.3-7.7X slower than the WebGL backend'; for Face Detector '~8.2-19.8X faster than the plain JS backend'. The tables give plain WASM vs plain JS from 3.0x (iPhone XS 140 vs 426.4 ms) to 12.1x (ThinkPad X1 Gen6 122.7 vs 1489.4 ms) for MobileNet V2 and 8.3x to 19.8x for Face Detector (derived from page data). With SIMD and threads, MacBook Pro 15 2019 MobileNet V2: 10.3 ms vs 893.5 ms plain JS (86.7x, derived from page data); ThinkPad X1 Gen6 12.4 ms vs 1489.4 ms (120x, derived from page data); Face Detector Desktop Linux 6.2 ms vs 249.5 ms (40x, derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: First-party Google numbers from Chrome 79 (2020), now old. The 'plain JS' baseline is TensorFlow.js's own unoptimized single-threaded CPU backend, not a native TensorFlow build; the 86.7x and 120x rows compare a multi-threaded SIMD build against that single-threaded JS. The README's '~5.3-7.7X slower than WebGL' text does not match its own table (Pixel 4 2.4x, ThinkPad 2.7x, Desktop Windows 3.0x slower), so the prose predates the current table. The Node v14 row was not measured in Chrome. Conv and matmul kernels come from XNNPACK, already listed in wave 8 (https://github.com/google/xnnpack). The benchmark page (tfjs-benchmarks.web.app) and the SIMD/threads blog post were not opened (egress blocked). Compiler flags and CPU models not stated. The tfjs-backend-wasm directory's last commit is 2024-04-12 (README typo fix; last code change 2023-09-20), while the repo-wide last commit is 2026-04-06 (a gsutil-to-gcloud chore).

notes: Numbers and quotes match the README; tier C confirmed.
